newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish pension reform needs more legislation - govt.
newsitem.headline: Polish pension reform needs more legislation - govt.

text.p: Poland's parliament, which this week adopted three key bills launching a vital pension reform, needs to quickly approve seven more if the overhaul is to start as planned in 1999, a government official said on Thursday.

The director of the government office in charge of the reform, Michal Rutkowski, said he was confident the new parliament, elected in the September 21 polls, would continue passing the social security bills. @
"In my opinion there is no possibility of stopping half way with the reform... I do not think that there is a possibility of calling off the reform," Rutkowski told a news conference.

The three social security reform bills, passed by the lower house of parliament on Wednesday, were backed by the ruling coalition of ex-communist and a peasant party along with the centre-right opposition.

The opposition Solidarity Election Action (AWS) -- a group now underrepresented in parliament but which has a chance of winning the elections, supports the reform in principle but wants to change many details.

Without the reform, Poland's public finances could collapse after 2004, due to the ageing of the population and inefficiency of the current pay-as-you-go system, inherited from the communist era before 1989, the government says.
The three adopted bills provide for creating new pension funds and using proceeds from privatisation of state-owned firms to finance the reform.

Under one bill, the government will be allowed to issue bonds convertible into shares of firms undergoing privatisation to gather funds for the reform, likely to cost about one percent of gross domestic product annually for 20 years. @
Rutkowski said the first such issue was likely in 1999 unless direct revenues from privatisation were large enough to cover the costs of the reform in that year.
He said the seven bills needed for the reform's completion should be approved by the end of the first quarter of 1998 if the reform is to be launched on January 1, 1999 as planned.

He said the bills would provide general regulations for the social security system, restructure the heavily subsidised Social Security Office (ZUS), now the sole pension provider, and regulate family and disability benefits as well as many other technical details. @

One of the planned bills, regulating levels of pensions for various occupations, is widely expected to cause controversy if the government pushes ahead with a plan to trim retirement privilages for certain groups, such as miners.
Rutkowski said the government was in no hurry to finish work on a controversial bill on reforming farmers' pensions -- the eighth and last of the key laws needed for the social security reform.
The farmers' pensions system functions separately and its overhaul can be delayed, Rutkowski said. @
The farmers' pension reform, which would curb the state subsidy for the so-called Farmers' Social Insurance Office (KRUS), is criticised by the co-ruling Peasant Party (PSL).
